newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Brazzaville nervous as Congo truce nears end.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville nervous as Congo truce nears end.

text.p: Red Cross workers are hoping to clear the streets of Brazzaville on Friday of the dead from 12 days of fighting, but some residents fear the weekend could bring new victims to replace them.
U.N. envoy Mohammed Sahnoun said African mediators in Gabon would ask the U.N. Security Council to support deployment of an inter-African force to help restore peace to the Congolese capital.
Rival factions have observed a cease-fire since midnight Tuesday and pledged to extend it for "as long as possible" after it officially ends at Friday midnight (2300 GMT).
But with no political solution in sight, and an apparent determination by France to pull out its sizeable force by the weekend, officials shared the nervousness of many residents.
"The weekend will be crucial, with only a very small and dwindling French presence left," a Western security officer in the city said by telephone.

In Gabon's capital Libreville, Sahnoun said that veteran Gabonese president Omar Bongo would ask the U.N. to support the proposed African force on behalf of mediators, who failed to rally warring parties around a peace plan on Monday.

Sahnoun, who visited Brazzaville on Wednesday for talks with rivals President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso, said the Organisation of African Unity would also be informed so that it could help.
France said on Thursday it would complete its pullout of 1,250 troops, who evacuated 5,700 foreign nationals, in the next few days despite pleas from Sahnoun for some to stay.
"If the entire operation goes as planned, (it) should be completed before Sunday, June 22," the defence ministry in Paris said.

Fighting erupted on June 5 when Lissouba tried to disarm the "Cobra" militia of Sassou Nguesso, his rival in elections that were to have been held on July 27. Lissouba ended 13 years of his ex-Marxist opponent's rule in free elections in 1992.
As the guns and artillery stayed quiet, more people on Thursday ventured out of the homes or other shelters in which the fighting had imprisoned them.

But the International Committee of the Red Cross, the only relief group still on the ground in Brazzaville, failed on Thursday to start its operation to help bury several hundred corpses that lie rotting where they were fell during the fighting.

"We have to co-ordinate through a ministerial committee for burial. There are medical-legal questions to be sorted out," ICRC spokesman Nick Sommer said. "We certainly hope it will start tomorrow (on Friday)."
Refugees, mainly West Africans with money to pay, continued to escape from Brazzaville in small numbers on Thursday, crossing the Congo River to Kinshasa in the former Zaire.
One said he had seen the Cobras burying their dead in his street.
"They'd buried 12 people and they were burying a 13th," he told reporters at a Kinshasa mosque where he found refuge. "They just bury them and write their names on the wall."
